children.text: The internet gave us a lot—streaming, social feeds, ways to work from anywhere. But it never quite figured out how to recreate something simple: a place you can show up, see who’s around, and spend time together.
That’s what’s starting to take shape in

. On any given week—whether it’s a Wednesday film screening, a Tuesday DJ set, or a Thursday night party—people log in because they know something’s happening and someone will be there. Some faces you start to recognize. Others are there for the first time, figuring it out just like you.
This is what happens when you build a party culture for the internet.
What Makes Online Parties in Decentraland Different

Most online events happen through a stream. You open a tab, press play, and watch alongside a large audience. There might be a chat moving quickly on the side, but it’s hard to tell who’s actually there or to have a real back-and-forth. You’re watching at the same time as everyone else, but you’re not really interacting.

Decentraland builds on that same format, but adds something that’s usually missing: a shared space. You don’t just press play, you arrive. You see who’s already there, start conversations before things begin, react together during the set, and stick around after because people are still talking. It feels closer to walking into a venue than opening a tab.

The key difference: the social layer stays intact. When you watch a DJ set in Decentraland Theatre, you're not in a chat with thousands of people you'll never see again. You're in a room where your avatar stands next to others, where text chat is happening in real time, and where the performer—their avatar actually present in the space—can see and respond to the crowd. It's the immediacy of being there without the logistics of actually traveling.
This matters more than it sounds. It’s the difference between watching something happen and being part of it.
The Party Types: What Actually Happens
People come to Decentraland for different kinds of gatherings. Not everything is a rave. Not everything is a concert. The range is one of the reasons people keep coming back.

Takeover Tuesdays is exactly what it sounds like: every Tuesday at 8pm UTC, a different Twitch streamer takes over Decentraland Theatre and plays a live set to a crowd that’s actually in the room. Recent sets have included artists like Austrian techno
, alongside a rotating lineup of DJs streaming live to both Twitch and the in-world audience—same moment, same energy, synced with lighting and effects inside the Theatre.

What makes this work: you’re in the room. The artist sees you. The crowd is your actual audience, not an abstraction. When Thug Shells is in the middle of a set and the Theatre lights up in sync, you’re experiencing that moment with people around you. The artist is present as an avatar, reacting to the room as much as the room reacts to the music.

Decentraland’s launch on the Epic Games Store
, with the room full of blue outfits and new faces arriving through Epic. May shifts into Cherry Blossom. June into Pride.
The format stays simple. Show up. Dress for the theme if you want. Dance. Talk to people.

New people arrive every month. Some are logging in for the first time. Others have been coming for a while and recognize each other right away. Someone brings a friend who wasn’t sure what to expect and ends up staying longer than planned. The energy comes from that mix—people returning, people figuring it out, all in the same space.

These parties are an easy entry point. No setup, no expectations beyond showing up. You can spend time on your outfit or not. You can talk or just hang back. Either way, it doesn’t take long to find your place in the room.

Each series shifts in theme. Previous lineups have included cult classics and horror films like

Here's what's interesting about this format: the film you're watching doesn't matter as much as the fact that
. Someone who came alone last week brings a friend this week. A group claims the same corner every Wednesday. The film is the reason you show up. The people are the reason you stay.

People drop in for one screening or follow the full series. The barrier to entry is so low that someone can show up on a whim, enjoy it, and come back next week. Or stay for the whole season. The structure doesn't demand anything. It just invites.
Recurring Community Hangouts and Smaller Gatherings

Not everything is a themed event or a scheduled show. Some of the most active social life in Decentraland happens in smaller, regular gatherings: campfire hangouts, conversations about emerging tech, creator workshops, and the kind of low-key hanging out that you can just show up for and join in.
Drop in any day of the week and you’ll find a whole host of community events that are open to everyone. The best place to start is by jumping into Genesis Plaza and checking out the Events tab.
Why People Keep Coming Back: It's Not About the Algorithm

This is the piece most online spaces miss. When you show up to the same party every week, you start recognizing people. You remember the person who always wears the metallic suit. The group that comes together from the same friend group. The new person who came for the first time last month and is now a regular.

That familiarity matters. It's the difference between "a crowd" and "your crowd." It's why people don't just attend events—they choose to be part of a particular scene. The Thursday night regulars are different from the Tuesday night crowd, which is different from the film festival audience. Each has its own personality.
Real DJs, Real Artists, Real Presence

When someone plays music in Decentraland, they're actually there. Their avatar is in the Theatre. They see the crowd. They're not a distant name on a livestream feed. The DJ can see 200 people dancing in the room, can read the chat, and can feel the energy.

This changes the artist's performance. A DJ playing to a crowd they can see—even an avatar crowd—performs differently than playing to an invisible audience. The connection is real. The feedback loop matters.

For the audience, it's equally different. You're not passive. You can chat with the artist. You can see your avatar react in the same space. You're part of the show in a way that simply watching a livestream never quite achieves.

One of the best things about Decentraland parties and experiences is what's missing: the algorithm. There's no engagement metric deciding whether you see an event announcement. There's no algorithm suppressing certain creators or boosting others based on invisible rules. There's no "recommended for you" deciding what should interest you.

The events happen on the calendar. They're announced. If you show up, you're in. The community decides what matters through attendance, not through platform optimization. This sounds small, but it changes everything about how social life functions.

People come back because the event will be there next week. Not because the algorithm is pushing them. Not because they're addicted to a notification. Not because they're afraid of missing out. They come back because it's good and because they know what to expect.
How to Show Up: It's Actually Simple
This might sound intimidating if you've never been to a virtual party before. It's not. You don't need to know people already. You don't need to prepare.

and jump in. You’ll land in Genesis Plaza, which acts as a starting point while you get your bearings.
From there, the next step is to check what’s happening. Open the Events tab in-world to see what’s live or coming up. That’s where the full schedule lives.
If something looks good, plan around it. Add it to your calendar. Show up when it starts. That’s when the space fills in and the experience clicks.
When you first arrive, you’ll be in a basic outfit. That’s completely fine—most people start there.
Once you’re in-world, you can start unlocking more options.

But none of that is required. People aren’t there for what you’re wearing—they’re there for who shows up.
Events run on a schedule, and timing matters. Arriving right as things start—or a few minutes before—makes it easier to settle in and catch the moment as it builds.

Take a seat in the Theatre. Dance the whole time. Text chat is always open. React to the music or the film. Comment on someone's avatar. Talk to people. Or just watch. There's no obligation to perform. You can be social or quiet. You can stay for 10 minutes or for the full duration.
Some people arrive solo. Some come with friends. Some show up every week. Some drop in once a month. There's no right way to experience it.
Beyond the Theatre: Where Else Parties Happen
The Theatre is the main venue you’ll find in Genesis Plaza, but it's not the only place where social gatherings happen in Decentraland. Parties and events also happen across:

LAND parcels: Throughout Genesis City, different property owners host events on their LAND. Some are clubs running their own party schedules. Some are galleries hosting launch parties. There is a huge variety of events to choose from.
Worlds: When someone claims a NAME in Decentraland, they

—a private digital space they can build and invite people into. Some people run their own recurring events in their Worlds. Private parties. Artist gatherings. Community meetings. These are smaller, more intimate, but often where the deepest social connections form.
The Bigger Picture: Why This Matters

There's something worth noticing about all of this. Online social spaces have been trying to solve the "how do we make people feel less lonely" problem for years. They've tried algorithms that recommend content. They've tried gamification. They've tried building elaborate feature sets. None of it quite works because presence itself is what's missing.

Decentraland takes a more straightforward approach. Make it easy for people to show up. Run events people can rely on. Let places become familiar over time. Make the crowd visible. Let people recognize each other. Let the social layer stay intact.

The result is that people come back. Not because something is pushing them to, but because they know what they’ll find when they arrive. The crowd is good. The space feels familiar. It feels like somewhere worth spending time.
This is closer to what people expected from the internet in the first place—a place you can return to, not just pass through.
If you're reading this and thinking "maybe I should try this," here's what to expect on your first night:

You'll arrive a little nervous. The space will feel new. You won't know what to do exactly. You'll figure out that walking is done with WASD keys. You'll find the Theatre. You'll stand around for a few minutes getting your bearings.
Then someone will chat with you. Or you'll realize the music is good. Or you'll notice the avatars are creative and weird and fun. And you'll think "okay, this is actually pretty cool."

Not everyone feels it right away. Sometimes it takes a second visit, or the right event, or recognizing a face from before. But if you do come back—if you show up to the next Thursday party or Tuesday set—you'll notice something different the second time. You'll recognize someone from last week. You'll know where to stand. You'll find your corner of the room. You'll realize that the person next to you is also here for the vibe, not for the feature set.
That's when it shifts. That's when it stops being "trying a virtual space" and starts being "this is my Thursday night."

The core truth: show up to a party. Stick around after. See who's there. Come back next week. That's how you find your crowd.

People ask what the appeal is. Why spend time in a virtual space when you could go to a real party? The honest answer: sometimes you can't. Maybe you're in a small town where there aren't parties like this. Maybe you have mobility issues. Maybe you're far from your friends. Maybe it's 2am and you're in a different time zone than your crew. Maybe you want to discover new music or communities without the friction of travel.
But sometimes you can go to a real party, and you still choose to log into
instead. That's when you know something is actually working.
The parties are good. The DJs are real. The crowd is there. You recognize people. The energy is good. The experience is frictionless. It feels like somewhere worth showing up to.
That's the thing about Decentraland's party culture that keeps growing. It's not replacing real parties. It's offering something that was missing online: an actual place to be together.

Decentraland Music Festival returns to Genesis City from Nov 19–22, 2025, and this year’s theme—SUB/STREAM—celebrates artists who made the stream their stage. Twitch icons, TikTok trailblazers, AI-native musicians, and virtual bands will unite in one global digital lineup. This year, two open calls invite both communities and performers to step into the lineup.
Streaming is where scenes are born and fandoms thrive. But what happens when your stream becomes a place—somewhere your audience can gather, move, and interact?

SUB/STREAM asks communities and creators to reimagine streaming as presence. The festival will pair global headliners with new talent, and transform underused parcels across Genesis City into long-lasting cultural spaces.
Open Call #1: Claim Your Party Pad

Party Pads are 2x2 festival home bases built for thriving digital communities—custom-built by professional Decentraland studios to spotlight fandoms, projects, and collectives. They’re not for solo creators but for groups with energy, culture, and an audience to bring. Think of them as clubhouses, lounges, or hubs where your crew shows up together and sets the vibe.
This is for you if your group is:
A fandom or streaming collective with regular live activations
An NFT or IP community looking to represent at the festival
A cultural crew or Discord server that already runs events
Any digital-native network with content and culture to share
From a Party Pad, communities can:
Stream DJ sets, talks, or fandom activations into the festival
Drop an exclusive Wearable for avatars Host watch parties, premieres, AMAs, or meetups
Showcase your Discord, collective, or project on the global stage
A fully-funded Party Pad build via Creator Connect
12 months of exhibition time in Genesis City
Festival map placement and official promotion
The strongest communities often come through existing networks. To highlight that, a new Referral Award has been introduced for the Party Pad Open Call.
Anyone can refer a community—whether it’s a fandom, cultural crew, Discord collective, or other digitally savvy network—to the Zealous application page.
When applying, the community includes the name and social media handle of the referral source.
If that community is selected as one of the six official Party Pads, the referral source will be contacted.
The reward is 500 MANA, awarded for each successful Party Pad referral.

You can refer as many communities as you like, but you’ll only receive the Referral Award if the successful Party Pad lists you in their application. If more than one referrer is mentioned, the award will be split between them.
Awards will be paid after the Party Pads are selected, with payment scheduled for Tuesday, Sept 30, 2025.

of Monday Sept 29, 2025, with the funds transferred to the wallet of your choice (ERC20) by Tuesday Sept 30, 2025. Payments will be made in MANA so an Ethereum wallet address is required.
This program recognizes the role the Decentraland community plays in connecting the festival with the most exciting digital collectives worldwide.
Open Call #2: Perform on the Main Stage
Eight new performers from the Decentaland community will join the Main Stage lineup alongside global stream-native pioneers.
This open call is looking for:
Twitch, TikTok, or YouTube Live artists expanding into 3D stages
Singer-songwriters, rappers, or instrumentalists already streaming originals
Performance artists blending music with visuals, avatars, or interactivity
$500 USD in MANA to support streaming setup
A 1-hour Main Stage slot during the festival
Promotion to Decentraland’s 600k+ social followers & 177k subscribers
Spotlight placement in the official program
Apply for a Main Stage slot
Decentraland Music Festival is more than a four-day event—it’s a chance to:
: Perform in a 3D festival space while simultaneously streaming to your existing channels.
: Party Pads and Main Stage builds remain live in Genesis City for at least 12 months.
: Previous festivals featured Deadmau5, Ozzy Osbourne, NGHTMRE, San Holo, and Whipped Cream. This year, you could be featured on the bill.
: The festival channels fans into Decentraland’s new Party-Goer Community, where activations continue year-round.

Before applying, download Decentraland and explore. No need to build yet—just get familiar with how activations feel in 3D space and check that your device runs the world smoothly. To be eligible, you’ll need to provide the email or wallet used to access Decentraland in your application.
Taking part in Decentraland Music Festival isn’t limited to award recipients. Even if you’re not selected for a Party Pad or Main Stage slot you can still be included in the official program.

The application form will include the option, “Even if I’m not selected, I’d still like to be part of the program.” This ensures every community and performer has the chance to be listed in the festival blog and lineup, with details that can be updated closer to the event.

The stage is set for stream-native culture to go collective. Whether you’re repping your community with a Party Pad or performing your set live on the Main Stage, this is your moment to turn streams into places and fandoms into destinations.
Submit by Sept 22, 2025 and be part of one of the most ambitious virtual music festivals dedicated to the stream-born generation.

This works well enough for scenes where the changes that you keep track of don’t happen continuously and where updates don’t need to happen immediately for everyone. But what if you want to keep track of something that is constantly moving and make sure that all players in the scene are seeing it in the same position?

Using WebSockets is the most robust solution if you want players to be in perfect sync with each other and it’s what most AAA multiplayer games use. In a WebSockets connection, data ‘frames’ can be sent at any time by the player or the server whenever there’s something to update.

A WebSockets connection is first established with a handshake between the player and the server which opens up a two-way stream of data to send and receive updates at any time, resulting in lower latency and better use of resources.

The Moonshot football stadium, where the Decentraland World Cup was held, is a perfect example of what’s possible thanks to WebSockets. Using WebSockets was essential to keep the ball’s position updated continuously and consistently for all players and spectators. Player positions were also synced via WebSockets to have less latency, their WebSocket-synced position was represented by an astronaut avatar to make them visible on all realms.

WebSockets provides more robust tools for ensuring that players don’t cheat, but you still need to do all the anti-cheating checks you’d do with a REST server. One advantage is that you only need to verify the player’s identity on the handshake stage, you don’t have to verify each request that the player sends. Another advantage is that once a session is open, you can be sure that all data coming in from that session is from the same source. For example, a cheating player wouldn’t be able to send fake requests to impersonate other players and mess with them.As with REST servers, the safest way to ensure that players don’t cheat is to have the game’s logic run server-side and make the game advance only through a specific sequence of actions that need to happen
